oil.summary: Crude surged sharply on Thursday as escalating Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz drove Brent back above $104 and WTI to $91.36. Reports of three tankers damaged in the Gulf and Iran's vow to block further Hormuz routes pushed supertanker rates to a record $1.4 million per day, with a large fleet tied up in ship-to-ship transfers outside the strait. Heating oil led the complex higher, up 6.84% on the day, reflecting tightening distillate supply routes. RBOB was the notable laggard, falling 2.09%, suggesting some demand-side caution stateside. On the supply side, Washington temporarily eased Russia oil sanctions to cool prices—a move that riled European allies—while India is pivoting away from Russian crude toward Middle East barrels as U.S. sanctions pressure bites. CME options markets price a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting.
drivers: Iranian tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz intensify, threatening Gulf export flows and driving supertanker rates to a record $1.4 million/day
U.S. temporarily eases Russia oil sanctions to dampen the price surge, while India shifts crude sourcing from Russia to Middle East suppliers
Heating oil +6.84% on distillate supply concerns; RBOB -2.09% diverges, signaling demand-side weakness in gasoline

gas.summary: Natural gas prices pulled back modestly on both sides of the Atlantic today—Henry Hub shed 1.37% to $3.159/MMBtu and TTF slipped 1.12% to €77.205/MWh—despite a strong weekly and monthly trend for Henry Hub (+6.47% and +11.94% respectively). The dominant headline was a Reuters exclusive reporting that the U.S. and Russia are actively exploring a framework to revive Russian gas sales to Europe, including a potential U.S. investor for the Nord Stream pipeline. The prospect of resumed Russian supply weighed on TTF sentiment at the margin. On the supply side, Equinor announced a new gas discovery at Norway's Gullfaks South field, with recoverable resources estimated at 3.3–10.3 million barrels of oil equivalent, offering incremental upside for North Sea production.
drivers: Reuters reports U.S. and Russia in discussions to revive Russian gas flows to Europe via a potential U.S.-backed Nord Stream investment, capping TTF upside
Henry Hub continues its strong monthly rally (+11.94%) even as today's session saw a modest pullback of -1.37%
Equinor discovers 3.3–10.3 MMboe of gas at Gullfaks South, supporting longer-term Norwegian North Sea supply outlook

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged higher, up 2.32% to $82.53, maintaining a steady uptrend over the past month (+1.68%). News flow in the power sector today was thematic rather than price-catalytic. A case study from California's September 9 heat event highlighted how over 140,000 home batteries discharged simultaneously through a virtual power plant, averting grid stress without new built capacity—a structural signal for demand-response investment. A drone attack on a UAE nuclear power plant was flagged as a headline risk. UK retailers urged government action to cut green levies as their collective electricity costs are set to rise £440 million this year, adding to policy pressure on power pricing. A separate commentary raised grid security concerns around Chinese long-duration batteries and foreign cyber threats. TTF's slight daily decline is a modest tailwind for carbon-linked power generation costs.
drivers: EU EUAs +2.32% to $82.53, sustaining a positive monthly trend as oil-linked energy crisis supports carbon pricing
California VPP event on Sept. 9 demonstrated 140,000+ home batteries discharging in coordination, underscoring distributed grid resilience as a scalable alternative to conventional capacity
UK retailers warn of £440 million electricity cost surge and press for green levy cuts; drone attack on UAE nuclear plant adds geopolitical risk to regional power supply
